Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) -- On the question of whether recent immigrants assimilate as quickly as previous waves, many Americans exhibit short fuses -- and even shorter memories. Ruben Navarrette Jr. notes that immigrants have been criticized throughout history for not assimilating. They have convinced themselves that, instead of adapting to the customs of this country, new arrivals -- most of whom come from Asia or Latin America -- expect the rest of us to accommodate them. They go ballistic over little things -- Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries that offer bilingual story time, or having to "press one for English." Yet, even as they look down on new immigrants, many Americans look back fondly upon their immigrant ancestors. Legend has it that when grandpa arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy or Poland, he jumped off the boat, immediately draped himself in the American flag, ripped out his native tongue, and abandoned his culture -- all while singing "Yankee Doodle Dandy." Germans did not move to Milwaukee and make beer and cheese. The Irish did not settle in Boston and join organizations like the Hibernian Society to preserve their heritage and culture. And even while Americans complain about how the current crop of immigrants aren't like their predecessors, they miss the irony: At the time, there were people who said the same thing about their ancestors; the Germans were thought to not be like the English, the Irish weren't like the Germans, the Italians weren't like the Irish etc. And the Chinese weren't like anyone who had come before them, and so they were labeled "unassimilable" by the Tom Tancredos of that era. Some things never change. When I was growing up in Central California, which is home to a large population of immigrants from Southeast Asia, thousands would gather to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would do a feature. And, in the days that followed, someone would write an angry letter to the editor complaining that these people weren't melting into the pot. Yet, there is more melting going on than one might think, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured three kinds of assimilation: economic (employment, education, homeownership, etc.); cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size, etc.); and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation, etc.). Far from discovering that recent immigrants are ducking the assimilation process, the study found that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival." Of course, individual groups still fall behind in some categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants have low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants have low levels of economic assimilation. And Canadian and Indian immigrants have low levels of civic assimilation, since few of them become citizens. But, overall, the news is good. After more than 200 years, America still does an excellent job of assimilating immigrants. Even if a particular group tried to resist the process, they wouldn't stand a chance. Assimilation happens, whether the immigrants are ready or not. Those are the facts. Of course, fear doesn't listen to facts. That is something else that hasn't changed. Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a member of the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) — On the question of whether recent immigrants assimilate as quickly as earlier waves, many Americans display short fuses—and even shorter memories. Ruben Navarrette Jr. observes that immigrants have been criticized throughout history for supposedly failing to assimilate.

Many Americans have convinced themselves that, rather than adapting to the customs of this country, new arrivals—most of whom come from Asia or Latin America—expect everyone else to accommodate them. They become incensed over small things: Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries offering bilingual story time, or having to “press one for English.”

Yet even as they look down on new immigrants, many Americans look back fondly on their own immigrant ancestors. Legend has it that when Grandpa arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy, or Poland, he leapt off the boat, immediately wrapped himself in the American flag, cast aside his native language, and abandoned his culture—all while singing “Yankee Doodle Dandy.”

In this nostalgic version of history, Germans did not move to Milwaukee and make beer and cheese. The Irish did not settle in Boston and join organizations such as the Hibernian Society to preserve their heritage and culture.

And even as Americans complain that today’s immigrants are not like their predecessors, they overlook the irony: At the time, people said the same things about their own ancestors. Germans were thought not to be like the English; the Irish were said to be unlike the Germans; the Italians were seen as different from the Irish; and so on. The Chinese, unlike anyone who had come before them, were labeled “unassimilable” by the Tom Tancredos of their era.

Some things never change.

When I was growing up in Central California, home to a large population of immigrants from Southeast Asia, thousands would gather to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would publish a feature on the event. In the days that followed, someone would inevitably write an angry letter to the editor complaining that these people were not melting into the pot.

Yet, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute, more melting is taking place than many might assume. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured three forms of assimilation: economic assimilation, including employment, education, and homeownership; cultural assimilation, including intermarriage, English proficiency, and family size; and civic assimilation, including citizenship, military service, and political participation.

Far from finding that recent immigrants are avoiding the assimilation process, the study concluded that “immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival.”

Of course, individual groups still lag behind in some categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants have low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants have low levels of economic assimilation. Canadian and Indian immigrants have low levels of civic assimilation, since relatively few of them become citizens.

Overall, however, the news is encouraging. After more than 200 years, America still does an excellent job of assimilating immigrants. Even if a particular group tried to resist the process, it would stand little chance. Assimilation happens, whether immigrants are ready for it or not.

Those are the facts. Of course, fear does not listen to facts. That, too, has not changed.

Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a member of the editorial board of the *San Diego Union-Tribune* and a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) — When it comes to the debate over whether today’s immigrants become part of American society as fast as earlier generations did, many Americans are quick to anger and slow to remember history. Ruben Navarrette Jr. points out that immigrants have always been accused of failing to assimilate.

Many people have persuaded themselves that newcomers — most of them from Asia or Latin America — are not adjusting to American traditions, but instead are demanding that everyone else adjust to them. They become furious over minor symbols and inconveniences: Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries holding bilingual story hours, or phone systems that ask callers to “press one for English.”

At the same time, many Americans who criticize today’s immigrants speak warmly about their own immigrant forebears. The romantic version suggests that when a grandfather arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy, or Poland, he stepped off the ship, wrapped himself in the American flag, gave up his native language on the spot, and cast aside his old culture — all while singing “Yankee Doodle Dandy.”

But that is not what happened. Germans did, in fact, settle in places such as Milwaukee and produce beer and cheese. The Irish did build communities in Boston and join groups such as the Hibernian Society to protect and celebrate their heritage.

And as Americans complain that modern immigrants are different from those who came before, they often overlook the irony: in earlier times, people made the same complaints about their own ancestors. Germans were viewed as unlike the English; the Irish were said to be unlike the Germans; Italians were considered unlike the Irish; and so on. The Chinese were seen as unlike any prior immigrant group and were branded “unassimilable” by the Tom Tancredos of that period.

Some patterns remain constant.

When I was growing up in Central California, an area with a large Southeast Asian immigrant population, thousands of people would come together to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would usually publish a story about the event. Then, in the following days, someone would send an angry letter to the editor insisting that these immigrants were not blending into the American melting pot.

But a new report from the Manhattan Institute suggests that more blending is taking place than many people assume. The study, described as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It examined three forms of assimilation: economic assimilation, including employment, education, homeownership, and related measures; cultural assimilation, including intermarriage, English ability, family size, and similar factors; and civic assimilation, including citizenship, military service, political involvement, and related indicators.

Rather than showing that recent immigrants are avoiding assimilation, the study concluded that “immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival.”

That does not mean every group performs equally well in every category. Chinese and Indian immigrants show low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants show low levels of economic assimilation. Canadian and Indian immigrants show low levels of civic assimilation because relatively few of them become citizens.

Still, the broader conclusion is positive. After more than two centuries, the United States continues to be highly effective at incorporating immigrants into its society. Even if one group attempted to resist assimilation, it would have little chance of succeeding. Assimilation takes place whether immigrants are prepared for it or not.

Those are the facts. But fear is not guided by facts. That, too, has not changed.

Ruben Navarrette Jr. serves on the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and is a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The views expressed in this commentary belong solely to the writer.

Many Americans criticize recent immigrants for not assimilating quickly enough, yet they often overlook the fact that earlier immigrant groups faced very similar accusations. Complaints that newcomers do not speak English, do not adopt “American” customs, or remain too attached to their homelands are not new. They have appeared repeatedly throughout U.S. history whenever large numbers of immigrants arrived from different cultural, linguistic, or religious backgrounds.

Navarrette argues that people frequently romanticize their own immigrant ancestors. In this nostalgic version of the past, earlier immigrants are imagined as having immediately embraced American culture, learned English overnight, and abandoned the traditions of the countries they came from. According to this view, today’s immigrants are different because they supposedly resist assimilation in ways previous generations did not. Navarrette challenges that assumption, suggesting that it is based more on selective memory than on historical fact.

In reality, many historical immigrant communities preserved important parts of their heritage for generations. German immigrants built German-speaking neighborhoods, published German-language newspapers, opened German schools, and maintained cultural traditions. Irish immigrants were often viewed with suspicion because of their Catholic faith and their political influence in cities. Italian immigrants kept their language, food, family customs, and religious traditions, and they too were often portrayed as outsiders. Chinese immigrants faced especially harsh discrimination and were described by many Americans as permanently foreign or unassimilable.

The same kinds of complaints heard today about immigrants’ languages, flags, foods, music, and cultural practices were directed at these earlier groups. Newcomers have long been accused of refusing to become American simply because they continued to speak their native languages, celebrate traditional holidays, or live in close-knit ethnic communities. Over time, however, many of these customs became accepted as part of American life. Foods, festivals, religious practices, and cultural traditions that were once considered foreign eventually became woven into the broader national identity.

Navarrette’s larger point is that fears about immigrant assimilation are cyclical. Each generation tends to believe that the newest immigrants are uniquely unwilling or unable to adapt, while forgetting that the same fears were once expressed about their own ancestors. Rather than reflecting a new crisis, modern anxieties about assimilation repeat old patterns. They are rooted in a selective memory of the past and a misunderstanding of how assimilation actually happens: gradually, unevenly, and often while immigrants continue to preserve parts of their original culture.

Critics often treat this as a new crisis, suggesting that recent immigrants are somehow different from earlier generations and less willing or able to become “American.”

Navarrette challenges that view by placing today’s complaints in a historical context. He argues that the same accusations have been made against many immigrant groups in the past. Earlier arrivals from Ireland, Italy, Germany, Eastern Europe, and other regions were also criticized for speaking foreign languages, living in ethnic neighborhoods, practicing unfamiliar religions, and maintaining traditions from their homelands. At the time, many native-born Americans feared that these groups would never fit into American society. Yet, over time, their descendants became widely accepted as part of the nation’s mainstream.

According to Navarrette, this pattern shows that the current backlash against Asian and Latin American immigrants is not evidence of a new failure to assimilate. Instead, it reflects a kind of historical amnesia. Americans often forget that their own ancestors were once viewed with the same suspicion now directed at newer immigrants. The process of assimilation has never meant that immigrants instantly abandon every part of their heritage. Rather, it has usually involved a gradual blending of identities, in which people learn English, participate in civic life, and adapt to American society while still preserving meaningful elements of their culture.

Navarrette’s larger point is that the fear of “unassimilable” immigrants is a recurring theme in American history. Each generation tends to imagine that the newest immigrants are uniquely resistant to becoming American, even though previous groups faced nearly identical criticism and eventually became part of the national fabric. By comparing present-day anxieties with past reactions to earlier immigrants, he suggests that today’s concerns are less about a genuine threat to American identity and more about forgetting how immigration and assimilation have always worked in the United States.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize Ruben Navarrette Jr.’s CNN commentary about whether modern immigrants assimilate as quickly as earlier immigrant groups, including the historical comparisons and the Manhattan Institute study findings.
counterfactuals.output:
Ruben Navarrette Jr.’s CNN commentary argues against the recurring claim that today’s immigrants—especially Latino immigrants—are not assimilating the way earlier immigrants did. He says that anxiety is not new: earlier waves of Irish, Italian, Jewish, Polish, German and other European immigrants were also accused of clinging to foreign languages, religions, neighborhoods and customs, and of threatening American identity. Over time, however, their children and grandchildren became accepted as “American,” and Navarrette suggests the same process is happening now.

He emphasizes that assimilation has never been instant. Earlier immigrants often lived in ethnic enclaves, published newspapers in their native languages, attended separate churches and faced suspicion from native-born Americans. Modern immigrants may look different because many are Latino and because immigration is more visible politically, but Navarrette argues the basic pattern—first generation struggles, later generations adapt—is historically familiar.

Navarrette cites a Manhattan Institute study, associated with researcher Jacob Vigdor, that measured immigrant assimilation across several dimensions, including cultural, economic and civic indicators. The study found that contemporary immigrants are assimilating at rates comparable to, and in some respects faster than, immigrants from the early 20th century. It noted progress in English acquisition, citizenship, homeownership, earnings and intermarriage over time, especially among the children of immigrants.

The commentary’s bottom line is that fears about modern immigrants refusing to assimilate are overstated. Navarrette frames today’s debate as a repeat of earlier nativist worries: Americans often doubt the newest arrivals, only to later recognize them as part of the national fabric.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed news-style summary of an opinion piece arguing that Americans unfairly accuse today’s immigrants of failing to assimilate while forgetting similar criticism of past immigrant groups.
counterfactuals.output:
An opinion piece argues that contemporary criticism of immigrants as unwilling or unable to assimilate repeats a long-standing American pattern: each new wave of newcomers is treated as uniquely resistant to becoming “American,” while earlier immigrant groups are later remembered as successful models of integration.

The writer contends that many Americans accuse today’s immigrants—often Latinos, Asians, Africans and people from the Middle East—of clinging to foreign languages, customs and identities. But, the piece says, nearly identical charges were once directed at groups now widely seen as part of the American mainstream, including Irish, Italian, German, Jewish, Polish and Eastern European immigrants.

According to the argument, critics in earlier eras warned that immigrants from Europe would never learn English, would remain loyal to foreign governments or religions, would crowd into ethnic neighborhoods and would weaken American culture. Irish Catholics were suspected of allegiance to the pope; Germans were criticized for maintaining their language and schools; Italians and Eastern European Jews were often portrayed as culturally alien and incapable of fitting into Anglo-Protestant norms. Over time, however, their descendants became accepted as fully American, and the prejudice they faced faded from popular memory.

The piece says this historical amnesia distorts today’s immigration debate. Americans often celebrate the assimilation of past immigrants while overlooking the fact that the process was gradual, uneven and frequently met with hostility. Ethnic newspapers, churches, mutual-aid societies, foreign-language schools and tight-knit neighborhoods were common among earlier groups, just as immigrant communities today maintain cultural institutions and family ties across borders.

The author argues that assimilation has rarely meant immediate abandonment of heritage. Instead, it has typically unfolded across generations: immigrants may retain their native language and customs, their children often become bilingual and bicultural, and later generations tend to identify strongly with the United States while preserving selected traditions. By that measure, the opinion piece says, many present-day immigrants are following the same path as earlier arrivals.

The piece also challenges the idea that assimilation requires cultural uniformity. It argues that American identity has repeatedly expanded as new groups entered the country and reshaped its food, politics, religion, music, labor force and civic life. What once seemed foreign often becomes familiar and eventually is treated as traditionally American.

At the same time, the writer suggests that accusations of failed assimilation often reveal more about the anxieties of the majority than about immigrants themselves. Concerns about language, religion, crime, work and national loyalty have been invoked repeatedly in U.S. history, particularly during periods of economic stress or rapid demographic change.

The opinion piece concludes that Americans should view today’s immigrants through a longer historical lens. Rather than assuming current newcomers are fundamentally different from those who came before, the author argues, the country should recognize that suspicion of immigrants has been a recurring feature of American life—and that many groups once denounced as unassimilable are now remembered as proof of the nation’s immigrant success story.

**Recap: Ruben Navarrette Jr. argues immigrant assimilation is more complex than critics claim**

In a column on immigrant assimilation, Ruben Navarrette Jr. pushes back against the recurring argument that newcomers to the United States are not adapting to American life. He suggests that much of the anxiety over assimilation is driven less by evidence and more by cultural discomfort — especially when immigrants publicly maintain ties to their heritage.

Navarrette points to examples often cited by critics: Mexican flags displayed at rallies or community events, bilingual government services, and cultural celebrations such as Hmong New Year. To some, he notes, these are treated as signs that immigrants are refusing to “become American.” But Navarrette argues that such symbols and accommodations do not necessarily undermine assimilation. Instead, they can coexist with immigrants learning English, working, raising families, and participating in civic life.

The column also references the **Index of Immigrant Assimilation**, a measure used to track how immigrants integrate economically, culturally, and civically over time. Navarrette uses the idea of such data to challenge the assumption that today’s immigrants are uniquely resistant to assimilation. Like earlier waves of newcomers, he suggests, many immigrants adapt across generations — even if the process is uneven and not always visible to those demanding immediate conformity.

His broader point: assimilation in America has never meant instant cultural erasure. Immigrants can celebrate their roots, speak more than one language, and still become part of the American mainstream.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: What is the main argument of Ruben Navarrette Jr.’s commentary on immigration assimilation, and what evidence does he cite from the Manhattan Institute report?
counterfactuals.output:
Ruben Navarrette Jr.’s main argument is that fears about immigrants—especially Latino immigrants—not assimilating into American life are exaggerated. He argues that assimilation is still happening, though it is gradual and uneven, and that immigrants generally become more American over time through language acquisition, work, citizenship, homeownership, and intermarriage.

He cites a Manhattan Institute report as evidence that immigrants are, in fact, integrating into U.S. society. The report measures assimilation in areas such as:

- **Cultural assimilation** — learning English, marrying outside one’s ethnic group, and adopting American social norms  
- **Economic assimilation** — employment, income growth, homeownership, and economic mobility  
- **Civic assimilation** — naturalization, military service, and participation in American institutions  

Navarrette points to the report’s findings that assimilation increases the longer immigrants live in the United States and that the children of immigrants tend to assimilate even more quickly. In other words, the evidence undercuts the claim that today’s immigrants are permanently separate from mainstream American society.
